lesson.title: Comparing Two Groups: The Two-Proportion Z-Test
lesson.summary: The two-proportion z-test compares proportions from two independent groups by pooling the data to estimate a single common proportion under the null hypothesis of no difference.
lesson.body:
Many real questions compare two groups rather than testing a single proportion against a claim: does a new website design get clicked more often than the old one, does one treatment succeed more often than another. The two-proportion z-test extends the one-proportion test you just learned to exactly this setting. The null hypothesis is typically H0: p1 = p2, equivalently p1 - p2 = 0, and the alternative is Ha: p1 not equal to p2, or a one-sided version if you have a directional prediction. Just as the confidence interval for a difference in proportions used phat1 and phat2 separately in its standard error, this test statistic compares phat1 - phat2 to the hypothesized value of 0, divided by a standard error.

The standard error, however, is built differently than it is for the confidence interval. Because H0 assumes the two population proportions are equal, the test statistic uses a single pooled proportion, phat_c, that combines both samples into one estimate of that common value: phat_c = (x1 + x2) / (n1 + n2), where x1 and x2 are the counts of successes in each sample. The standard error under H0 is then the square root of phat_c(1 - phat_c) times (1/n1 + 1/n2). This mirrors the exact same logic from the one-proportion test: when you assume H0 is true, you should use the value implied by H0, here a single shared proportion, everywhere the standard error calls for a proportion, rather than plugging in the two separate sample proportions you actually observed.

Suppose a company tests two versions of a website. Version A is shown to 200 visitors, and 45 of them click a signup button, phat_A = 45/200 = 0.225. Version B is shown to a different, independently sampled 200 visitors, and 60 of them click, phat_B = 60/200 = 0.30. Is this a statistically significant difference at alpha = 0.05. First pool the samples: phat_c = (45 + 60)/(200 + 200) = 105/400 = 0.2625. The standard error under H0 is the square root of (0.2625)(0.7375)(1/200 + 1/200), which works out to the square root of 0.00194, or about 0.0440. The test statistic is z = (0.225 - 0.30) / 0.0440 = -1.70. For a two-sided test, the p-value is 2 times P(Z < -1.70), which is about 2(0.045) = 0.089. Since 0.089 is greater than alpha = 0.05, this sample does not provide convincing evidence, at the 0.05 level, of a real difference between the two versions. Notice that the observed gap, 22.5 percent versus 30 percent, looks meaningful, but with these sample sizes it is not strong enough evidence to rule out that the difference is just sampling variability.

The conditions for a two-proportion z-test parallel the one-proportion case: both samples need to arise from random sampling or random assignment, the two groups need to be independent of each other as well as internally, and the Large Counts condition needs to hold in each group, using the pooled proportion phat_c in place of p0. In the website example, n1(phat_c) = 200(0.2625) = 52.5 and n1(1 - phat_c) = 147.5, with the same values applying to group 2 by symmetry, all comfortably above 10, so the normal approximation is trustworthy here.
